title: Stop Using Plausibility as the Criterion for Explainable AI
claim: Optimizing explanations for human plausibility pushes them toward misleading regions, hiding the bias-detection and decision-verification roles explanations should serve.
layout: 1 central 2D plot with four corner example boxes; diagonal band device
description: A conceptual 2D plane. The x axis, labeled 'AI model', runs from wrong prediction to right prediction. The y axis, labeled 'XAI algorithm', runs from implausible reason to plausible reason. A large green diagonal band, 'Decision verification zone', crosses the plane. A yellow 'Misleading zone' triangle sits at top-left. A blue 'Bias detection zone' sits at bottom-right, with a lighter 'Knowledge discovery zone' in the corner. Quadrants are numbered I–IV. A red dotted line and red upward arrow mark the effect of optimizing XAI for plausibility. A green arrow marks the effect of optimizing the AI for plausibility. Four gray-headed example boxes (I–IV) sit at the corners. Each shows a bee photo with a user question and an AI answer, such as 'long antennae' or 'toothbrush'. The eye goes first to the colored zones.
caption: The conceptual 2D distribution diagram of AI explanations from an XAI algorithm regarding the probability of AI prediction correctness ($x$ axis) and the degree of plausibility ($y$ axis).
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is motivated by the problem of making AI predictions understandable, transparent, and responsible, as AI becomes increasingly impactful in society and high-stakes domains. The evaluation and optimization criteria of XAI are gatekeepers for XAI algorithms to achieve their expected goals and should withstand rigorous inspection. To improve the scientific rigor of XAI, we conduct the first comprehensive and critical examination of a common XAI criterion: plausibility. Plausibility assesses how convincing the AI explanation is to humans, and is usually quantified by metrics of feature localization or feature correlation. Our examination shows that plausibility is an invalid measure of explainability, and human explanations are not ground truth for XAI, because both ignore the necessary assumptions of explanation. One fundamental assumption is that AI explanations are supposed to behave adversarially, analogous to auditors' or doctors' roles of identifying potential problems. Evaluating or optimizing XAI to generate more plausible explanations is analogous to incentivizing (i.e., bribing) auditors/doctors to generate more positive reports, which is different from encouraging AI models to learn more plausible features (analogous to encouraging companies/patients to improve their conduct/health). Our examination further reveals the consequences of using plausibility as the XAI criterion, including increasing misleading explanations that manipulate users, deteriorating users' trust in the AI system, undermining human autonomy, being unable to achieve complementary human-AI task performance, and abandoning other possible approaches of enhancing understandability. Due to the invalidity of measurements and the unethical issues, this paper argues that the AI community should stop using plausibility as the criterion to evaluate and optimize XAI algorithms.
